transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-08-16
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 mins
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Zenith CTO), Aaron Chen (Zenith ML Eng), Priya Nair (Zenith Infra), Samir Gupta (Zenith PM)

Summary:
- Scoping call to agree on POC success criteria focused on latency/throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), measurement plan, workload sizing and timelines.
- Zenith wants predictable tail latency for chat and embeddings workloads; evaluating hosted first then Dedicated if needed.

Topics covered:
- Definitions: TTFT (time to first token), TPOT (time per output token) and how they map to p95/p99 targets
- Measurement plan: synthetic load vs replay of real prompts, warmup, KV cache hit scenarios, cold-start vs steady-state
- Benchmarks: single-request latency, batched throughput, token throughput, concurrency and tail behavior
- Timeline and deliverables for POC

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros, i'm maya from redwood, diego from infra will run the bench stuff; who do we have over there?
[00:08] Lena: lena here, cto, we want to validate latency for our chat service and also batch embedding job, hi all.
[00:15] Aaron: aaron ML eng, i'll share prompts and we care about tail 99s, um, because some user journeys are very latency-sensitive.
[00:22] Priya: priya infra, i'll be the one who schedules the load windows and handles networking.
[00:30] Diego: awesome. quick agenda: agree success criteria, define concrete p95/p99 numbers for TTFT/TPOT, agree measurement harness, and timeline.
[01:02] Maya: as a starting point, can you share current numbers? like what are you seeing in prod?
[01:10] Lena: so for our chat, average first token is ~120ms but tail p99 spikes to 900ms during peak, that's from our current self-hosted service on GPU instances, and embeddings batch jobs run within a few minutes but we're billed per-token and want to optimize.
[01:28] Diego: when you say p99 900ms is that cold-start or steady state?
[01:32] Aaron: mostly steady-state; we think there's queueing and batching configuration issues, also kv cache misses for long context.
[01:40] Maya: good, that maps to the two vectors we'll measure: cold-start/scale events and steady-state tail under load. also, we need to be explicit about TTFT vs TPOT — ttft is the time to first token, which matters for perceived latency; tpot is time per output token, which matters for streaming responses.
[02:05] Samir: quick q — do you measure tokens as utf-8 tokens or tokenized by model?
[02:09] Diego: good question, tokenization is model-dependent; our benchmark reports tokens based on the model tokenizer (so token counts are consistent).
[02:17] Maya: proposed success criteria (tentative):
- Chat TTFT: p95 < 250ms, p99 < 500ms for typical short prompts (<= 80 tokens).
- Chat TPOT: p95 < 18ms/token, p99 < 45ms/token for streaming generation.
- Embeddings batch latency: per-request (100 items) p95 < 2s, p99 < 5s.
- SLO measurement: p95/p99 computed over 15-min windows during 1-hour test runs, plus at least one 4-hour soak to capture diurnal effects.
[03:05] Lena: p95 < 250 seems reasonable, p99 < 500 is a big improvement from 900ms, are these realistic on your hosted plan?
[03:14] Maya: yes for many models on our hosted clusters we can hit those with proper batching and warm KV cache, but it depends on model size and prompt mix. for larger models or cold cache, p99 will be higher; if you need strict p99 we typically recommend dedicated capacity or reserved nodes.
[03:35] Aaron: what's your approach to measuring cold starts? we got burned by scale events during big campaigns.
[03:41] Diego: we simulate scale by booting new worker pods and then sending a burst; measurement distinguishes request queueing time vs model load time. we'll instrument time-since-request-enter-queue, time-to-dock-model, and first-token emission.
[03:58] Maya: also important — KV cache hit rate: we'll run tests with 0%, 50%, and 90% cache hit mixes because when you have prefix caching the TTFT can be dramatically lower.
[04:12] Priya: on the VPC/private side, we care about network egress and cold-start time if you need to pull model artifacts behind our firewall. how does private compare?
[04:22] Diego: private deployments add artifact fetch time and sometimes slower model load due to air-gapped storage, so cold-starts can add ~200-400ms depending on infra; but steady-state is comparable. we document that in our private deployment notes.
[04:40] Maya: measurement plan details:
- Inputs: Zenith will provide 1k representative prompts (Aaron) split into short/medium/long contexts.
- Warmup: 10-minute warmup to populate KV cache and JIT paths.
- Runs: three 1-hour runs at target QPS levels (low, mid, peak) plus a 4-hour soak at mid load.
- Metrics: TTFT (request-level first-token latency), TPOT (per-output-token time measured across tokens 2..N), p95/p99 for both, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, batch size distribution, and queueing time.
[05:30] Samir: what about measurement tooling? we prefer k6 but ok to run your harness.
[05:35] Diego: we have a benchmark harness (internal) that can replay prompts with timings and produce per-request traces; for reproducibility we'll export k6 scripts too. we'll include the raw logs and a spreadsheet.
[05:47] Maya: Diego will run an initial baseline in hosted env with the same model you intend to use (please confirm model size).
[05:55] Aaron: we plan to test the 7B and 13B variants, mainly 13B in prod.
[06:01] Diego: noted — 13B will have different TPOT. expected numbers on 13B: TTFT p95 ~200-300ms hosted with warm cache, TPOT p95 ~25-35ms/token but we'll validate.
[06:15] Lena: ok can you explain how you compute TPOT — is it averaged over tokens or sliding window?
[06:20] Diego: we compute per-token latency for tokens 2..N then report percentiles across all token observations; TPOT p95 means 95% of token emissions were <= value. we also report token-latency broken down by token position (first 20 vs rest) because early tokens often incur extra overhead.
[06:38] Aaron: how do batching and concurrency affect TTFT? we have a lot of small requests so batching might increase TTFT.
[06:44] Maya: yes batching trades off latency for throughput; our runtime supports small-batch fast paths and continuous batching; in the measurement we'll sweep batch sizes and concurrency to find sweet spot. one of the POC goals is to tune batching/policy to meet your SLO while minimizing cost.
[07:03] Priya: cost matters. if dedicated is needed for strict p99 we want to see cost delta.
[07:08] Maya: we'll include estimated unit cost (token and GPU hour) for each tested config.
[07:14] Samir: what about quantization or lower precision to speed up TPOT?
[07:19] Diego: we can test INT8/4-bit quantized variants; TPOT often improves significantly with quantization but may affect quality. we'll include quality checks (perplexity and a small eval set) in the bench.
[07:33] Maya: Quality regression check: Aaron, can you provide 50 eval prompts we can use to confirm output fidelity across quantized/model variants?
[07:40] Aaron: yes will do.
[07:42] Maya: success criteria recap (we'll include in doc):
- Primary: Chat TTFT p95 < 250ms and p99 < 500ms on target model (13B) with representative prompt mix and >80% KV cache hit scenario.
- Secondary: TPOT p95 < 20ms/token (stretch 18ms), p99 < 45ms/token.
- Embedding batch p95 < 2s for 100-item batch.
- Cost: estimated per-token cost within X% of current baseline (we'll compute).
[08:20] Lena: acceptable, want to see both hosted and dedicated options with costs and SLA differences.
[08:28] Diego: measurement details again — we'll collect: request_id, timestamp, model_version, node_id, batch_size, queue_wait_ms, model_load_ms, kernel_choice, kv_cache_hit (boolean), first_token_latency_ms, per_token_latencies_ms array, and we'll produce aggregated p95/p99 tables.
[08:53] Priya: are those logs safe to share? we need to redact user data.
[08:57] Maya: yes we'll only log prompt hashes and no PII; Redwood follows SOC2 practices — we'll attach security docs.
[09:06] Samir: will you include charts for latency over time and waterfall traces?
[09:10] Diego: yes, per-request waterfall traces for slow tail requests to debug cause (queueing vs model vs network).
[09:16] Aaron: on distribution — how do we model variable prompt lengths?
[09:20] Diego: you'll give us percentiles of prompt lengths (p50/p90/p99) and we'll replay with matching distribution; also test extreme long contexts separately to exercise KV cache and memory pressure.
[09:35] Maya: timeline proposal:
- 2027-08-18: benchmark template and security docs to Zenith (Maya)
- 2027-08-19: Zenith provides sample prompts + VPC details (Zenith)
- 2027-08-23: Redwood runs baseline hosted tests and shares raw logs and summary (Diego)
- 2027-08-25: joint review and decision on whether dedicated needed; schedule load window if yes.
[10:05] Lena: sounds good. we have one more concern — p99 SLA, do you provide autopolicy fallback? e.g., if hosted is under pressure route to larger nodes?
[10:14] Maya: yes we have smart routing and fallback options; in Dedicated you can reserve capacity and enable overflow to hosted with fallback policies. we'll include routing playbook in the doc.
[10:24] Priya: networking question: during load tests we need to ensure MTU and TLS handshake times are stable. should we provision long-lived connections to reduce handshake overhead?
[10:33] Diego: yes long-lived connections and keep-alive reduce per-request overhead; we'll test both keep-alive and new-conn scenarios.
[10:40] Samir: any other blockers?
[10:43] Aaron: none from my side if we get templates.
[10:45] Maya: OK, quick recap and next steps — i'll send the template and pricing, diego will run baseline and share logs, priya will confirm networking window.
[10:58] Lena: thanks all.
[11:00] Maya: thanks, speak soon.

Appendix - Measurement plan (notes):
- p95/p99 windows: compute percentiles across per-request first-token latencies and per-token latencies across aggregated token observations; for embeddings compute per-request end-to-end time.
- Windows and sample sizes: minimum 10k requests per run to get stable p99 estimates; run three independent 1-hour tests plus a 4-hour soak.
- Load profiles: low (10% expected peak QPS), mid (50%), peak (100%); include bursts to emulate scale-up.
